newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Kidd weighs disclosure rules for power firms.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Kidd weighs disclosure rules for power firms.

text.p: New Zealand Energy Minister Doug Kidd said on Wednesday that the government was considering tougher disclosure rules for power companies to sharpen competition in electricity retailing.

"My officials are currently giving active consideration to proposals for strengthening the information disclosure regulations," Kidd said in a speech at the annual meeting of the Electricity Supply Association.

"There are proposals to tighten the guidelines for allocating costs, revenues, assets and liabilities amongst companies' business units and to make the guidelines mandatory. This more tightly ring-fences the lines business and makes cross-subsidisations more transparent."
Kidd said this should be a "salutary warning" to power companies, a number of which had taken advantage of the fact that current guidelines were not mandatory.
"If you can't, or won't, act responsibly and regulate yourselves, you leave this and future governments with no option but to crank up the regulatory regime," he said.

One proposal was to require electricity retailers to disclose details of the way in which they allocate costs and revenues between domestic and business customers to ensure that the former got a fair deal.

The adoption of profile metering -- where domestic consumers are billed half-hourly according to an average use profile for their region -- could significantly increase the level of retail competition, he said.

"I challenge you to develop a metering solution as soon as possible. If the industry does not take the initiative, this matter may be taken out of the industry's hands as there will be strong pressure on the government to protect domestic consumers."

Kidd said he was pleased that electricity companies appeared to have heeded his warning in August 1994 that he was concerned about excessive fixed charges. Those with the highest charges had subsequently reduced them.

He said he had some reservations about the way Trans Power had recently announced its pricing proposals. "Trans Power needs to confer closely with its customers and be able to fully justify any proposals that it develops."
Kidd said he was confident the benefits of the new wholesale electricity market from October 1 would be far-reaching, and it would place its own strict disciplines on new investment.
"Those who build new stations have the incentives to get it right...The disciplines on new investment alone will deliver real long-term benefits," he said.
